name: First-wave feminism
summary: First-wave feminism, from the late eighteenth century to the 1920s, demanded formal legal and political equality for women: the vote, the right of married women to hold property and earnings, access to education and the professions, and fairer marriage and divorce law. Its basis was Enlightenment and liberal natural-rights thought applied to women, pursued mostly by petition, organisation and persuasion, with civil disobedience and militancy in some countries. It left economics, foreign policy and most other questions open, and its leaders were often middle-class, with racial and class divisions.
scope: The Anglo-American and wider liberal women's-rights movement from Wollstonecraft (1792) through Seneca Falls (1848), Mill's Subjection of Women (1869) and the suffrage campaigns up to about 1920. It excludes the later second-wave and radical, socialist and intersectional feminisms. Most non-gender statements are anachronistic or never addressed and are marked low-confidence inferences.

sources.usedFor: Abolitionist roots, Fifteenth Amendment split, temperance, racist arguments, civil disobedience and militancy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; the movement's demands were legal and political, and the sources record no stance on state medicine.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Declaration protests women's scanty pay and exclusion from trades, but wage floors were not a demand; adherents were divided between middle-class reformers and labour-linked women.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Economic doctrine was not the movement's concern; its liberal wing took market economies for granted while socialist-leaning women in Germany and Argentina did not.

public-ownership.rationale: The mainstream, liberal and middle-class movement did not call for nationalisation; only its socialist-leaning minority would, so a mild no is inferred.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: No documented position; Stanton's wish to enfranchise wealthy women shows concern with class standing, not tax policy.

unions-good.rationale: Suffrage groups in Norway and Germany split over bourgeois versus working-class membership, so attitudes to organised labour varied and no common line is documented.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Declaration's central property grievance is that a married woman loses all right in property and even her wages, so securing women's property rights was a core demand within a liberal frame.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporate regulation did not figure in the movement's programme; nothing in the sources decides it.

cut-welfare.rationale: No stance recorded; moral-reform wings favoured charity and relief work while liberals favoured limited government, so it is split.

worker-ownership.rationale: The liberal mainstream sought equal rights within existing property relations; worker ownership was a socialist side-strand, so a weak no is inferred.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the movement's liberal rights framework speaks to counter-terror surveillance.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Many suffragists were temperance advocates, with the WCTU the largest women's organisation of its day, so legal drug availability is inferred as disfavoured.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Anachronistic; liberal free-expression instincts and a concern for the dignity of the excluded pull in opposite directions.

strong-leader.rationale: Mill likens domestic and political despotism and rejects arbitrary power; adherents would distrust a leader who bypasses legislatures, which the movement was trying to enter.

state-harmful.rationale: The movement demanded entry into the state's franchise and legal protection, so the claim that the state is harmful and unnecessary runs directly against its programme.

limit-guns.rationale: No documented position; temperance-era moral reformers leaned to restriction, liberal rights thinking the other way.

empower-police-military.rationale: Wollstonecraft holds that standing armies are incompatible with freedom, and the movement had no interest in expanding coercive forces; inferred weakly.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Nineteenth-century feminists attacked the sexual double standard and many joined social-purity campaigns, so legalisation would not be endorsed; the sources do not state the point directly.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement fought for national and state-level suffrage and law reform rather than a devolution principle, though campaigns were often won state by state.

rehabilitation.rationale: Moral-reform and temperance feminists generally favoured reform of offenders over pure punishment; inferred rather than documented.

traditional-family.rationale: Mill attacks the husband's legal despotism in the family and wants marriage between equals, though many first-wave women valued home and motherhood, so the rejection is mild.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The movement never raised it and its 19th-century moral framework assumed marriage between a man and a woman; anachronistic, inferred weakly.

abortion-legal.rationale: The agenda in some countries included contraception and abortion, but leading American and British suffragists mostly opposed abortion, so a weak no is inferred.

more-religion-public.rationale: Adherents were split: Declaration signers protest church-sanctioned subordination, yet Catholic and temperance-Christian women were part of the movement.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Leaders came out of abolitionism, but the Fifteenth Amendment split and Stone's line that woman must wait for the Negro show adherents divided on racial equality.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Mill argues that what is called women's nature is an eminently artificial thing shaped by subordination, which is a social-construction claim, though he does not deny all natural difference.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Not a movement concern; Nationalist and internationalist strands, such as the International Alliance of Women, coexisted.

gradual-change.rationale: Strategies ranged from petitions and salons to militancy and civil disobedience such as Anthony's 1872 vote, so adherents split on pace and respect for institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Stanton disparaged immigrant voters, but no movement-wide immigration policy existed.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Suffragists built international alliances, but the question of empowering bodies like the UN postdates the movement.

free-trade.rationale: No documented position; economic policy was outside the movement's remit.

nation-first.rationale: Not addressed; national suffrage campaigns coexisted with an international alliance.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Anachronistic; adherents' views on foreign intervention are not documented.

open-borders.rationale: Nothing endorses open borders, and some prominent suffragists were hostile to immigrant voters; weak no inferred.

limit-growth.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement predates environmental limits-to-growth debates.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; no position can be derived.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No stated view; Enlightenment faith in progress cuts one way, moral-reform scepticism of modernity the other.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis for an answer.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Declaration borrows the Declaration of Independence's language of throwing off despotism, but the movement mostly worked by petition and agitation, so adherents split.

experts-over-public.rationale: Mill opposes rule by custom and presumption and demands the vote for women as the public; the movement argued for wider participation, so a weak no is inferred.

central-planning.rationale: A centrally planned economy was not a first-wave aim; the liberal mainstream is inferred to reject it.

socialized-markets.rationale: Economic structure was not part of the programme and the movement had both liberal and socialist wings.

land-value-tax.rationale: No documented stance on single-tax proposals.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Wollstonecraft criticises hereditary riches and rank, but the movement also demanded women's equal right to inherit and hold property.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The liberal mainstream did not look to the state to steer investment; inferred weakly.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The demand that married women hold property and earnings fits wide personal property ownership, though no source states the broader proposition.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The Declaration protests that women are paid scantily and denied wages of their own, and demands access to paid professions, so abolishing wages contradicts the programme.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions never appear in the sources on women's suffrage or legal reform, so no position can be derived.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies setting wages jointly was not a first-wave proposal; the movement's individual-rights frame implies a weak no.

one-party-rule.rationale: The movement fought for the equal franchise and representation, and Mill attacks despotism, so rule by a single party is clearly rejected.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Wollstonecraft blames monarchy and hereditary rank for much misery, though many suffrage campaigns ran in monarchies and did not oppose them as such.

democracy-best.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments grounds its demand in the principle of consent and representation, and the vote was the movement's defining aim, so democratic government is central.

direct-votes.rationale: Suffragists sought the franchise for women and often supported referendums on suffrage, but no stance on direct legislation is documented.

workers-councils.rationale: Entry into parliament and the electorate was the programme, so replacing parliaments with councils is contrary to it.

right-to-secede.rationale: The movement campaigned for rights within existing states and said nothing on secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Wollstonecraft and Mill reject any natural fitness of men to rule women, but Mill backed plural votes for the educated and Stanton argued for educated suffrage.

political-violence-never.rationale: Most early suffragists were non-violent petitioners, but later militants jailed in 1917 and British suffragettes adopted forceful tactics, so adherents split.

war-builds-character.rationale: Wollstonecraft treats standing armies as hostile to liberty and virtue; inferred weakly for the whole movement.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Declaration protests subordination of women in Church as well as State and treats conscience as private, which suggests a liberal separation, though Christian women's groups were part of the movement.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Declaration rejects the claim of apostolic authority to exclude women from the ministry and the laws that rest on subordination, so scripture-derived law is resisted.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The movement demanded equal legal protection through public courts; private justice is not discussed.

military-superiority.rationale: Defence posture was outside the movement's concerns, apart from Wollstonecraft's dislike of standing armies, so it is left neutral.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The universal-rights basis of the movement is at odds with ethnic nationhood, though Stanton and others voiced prejudice; weak no.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The mainstream movement was liberal and legalistic, and splits over class in Norway and Germany show class conflict was not its account of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: First-wave feminism sought formal equality, in contrast with the substantive equality that later waves sought, so equal outcomes is not its goal.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The movement's sources do not discuss indigenous peoples or land authority.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Not addressed; critics note first-wave feminism accepted colonial hierarchies.

civilizational-union.rationale: Unions of nations by religion or civilization are not discussed in any first-wave source opened.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Mill's liberal ethics value individual choice but he attacks selfishness fostered by domestic despotism, so there is no clear line.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Declaration is a claim of inalienable rights against communal custom, and Mill makes individual choice central, so duties-first is the opposite stance.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental ethics is absent from first-wave writings, so no answer can be inferred.

limit-population.rationale: Birth-control campaigners such as Jacobs sought women's control over fertility, not population targets, so it is not answerable.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movement's demands for education and paid professions presuppose modern society.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The sources contain no stance on speeding up technological change at the cost of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily enhancement by technology is anachronistic for a movement that ended around 1920.

algorithmic-government.rationale: AI governance is anachronistic and has no basis in first-wave principles beyond a general liberal preference for accountable human representation.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Anachronistic; a liberal privacy instinct is the only guide.

restore-past-order.rationale: Mill argues that custom is no evidence of soundness and that unnatural means only uncustomary, directly rejecting restoring a lost order over reform.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Mill advocates utility but the movement's arguments rested on principle of equal rights, so it is split.

direct-action.rationale: Most work went through petitions and lobbying for the vote, but Anthony's arrest for voting and the 1917 pickets show direct action also used.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The movement demanded access to education, professions and the vote within modern society, so a return to foraging is contrary.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Mill would let spouses divide tasks by agreement according to ability, which keeps division of labour but frees it from sex, so abolition is not the stance.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The programme demanded the right to earn and own wages, implying reward by work; weak no.

production-for-use.rationale: Not a first-wave idea; the liberal mainstream is inferred to accept profit-making.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Marxist exploitation theory belongs to the socialist wing only; the mainstream is inferred to disagree.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The movement sought equal rights through the franchise, not dictatorship by any class.

taxation-theft.rationale: The Declaration protests taxation without representation, since women are taxed but not heard, which accepts taxation as legitimate when representative.

harm-principle.rationale: Mill, the movement's leading liberal theorist, authored the harm principle, though temperance and moral-reform feminists wanted legal restrictions on drink and vice beyond it.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Declaration frames rights as inalienable rights of each person, though German feminism stressed collective representation, so the view is not unanimous.

conscription.rationale: Wollstonecraft says standing armies conflict with freedom; no source speaks of conscription directly.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The movement's defining demand was the vote, and the Declaration treats denial of the franchise as the central wrong, so voice outranks exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Not discussed; the citizen-as-customer idea is foreign to a rights-based movement.

positive-liberty.rationale: Formal equality was the aim, though education and economic access demands imply a material side; adherents are split.

economic-freedom.rationale: The demand for wages, property and professions is an economic-freedom claim, but sources do not tie it to political freedom as the statement does.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not a first-wave claim; universities were closed to women, so adherents saw them as lacking power over them rather than holding it.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Mill's thesis is that unequal capacities are produced by circumstances rather than nature, a stance against hereditarian claims, though some suffragists voiced racist views.

organic-representation.rationale: The movement demanded individual votes for women, not representation through families or corporate bodies.

total-state.rationale: The movement claimed rights against the state's customs and laws, and the Declaration treats conscience as the individual's own, so total direction is rejected.

national-rebirth.rationale: No such theme appears in the movement.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Wollstonecraft ties armies and rank to misery; expansion not endorsed.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Mill likens rule by personal power to despotism and champions consent-based law.

bound-labor.rationale: The Declaration condemns laws that bind a married woman to obedience and civil death, and the movement came out of abolitionism, so bound labour is rejected.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Mill holds that reason can tell truth from custom, so the radical claim that all knowledge reflects power is not his; later wave idea.

universal-morality.rationale: Wollstonecraft says truth must be common to all and Seneca Falls invokes natural law, supporting universal moral truths known by reason.

single-common-good.rationale: German feminism spoke of a political common good, while liberal strands balanced interests, so views vary.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return rights were no part of the women's-rights agenda.

revive-national-language.rationale: Finnish and other nationalist-aligned feminists may have supported it, but there is no movement view.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democratic control of firms was a socialist theme; the sources show the mainstream movement silent on it.

school-vouchers.rationale: The movement wanted state-supported education for girls, but vouchers are not discussed.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was never taken up by the suffrage and legal-reform movement.

rule-by-example.rationale: Mill demands equal laws, not reliance on rulers' moral example; Wollstonecraft criticises rank.

national-self-determination.rationale: Not addressed beyond some Finnish and Chinese national contexts.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN did not exist during the movement, and no principle in the sources settles unilateral force.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Wollstonecraft says reason and virtue raise humans above animals and denounces sensibility, but she defends a religious frame, so the statement's exclusive claim is only partly shared.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare eligibility for immigrants was not raised by first-wave campaigners.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Work conditions on relief were not a feminist issue in the period, and the sources give no line.

class-collaboration.rationale: The mainstream movement was middle-class and reformist, seeking cooperation rather than class war, though socialist women disagreed.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The movement demanded entry to colleges, libraries and professions, so destroying inherited institutions runs against it.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western fronts of dominated countries are unrelated to the movement's concerns.

workers-nation.rationale: National versus international organising of workers was a socialist debate, not a first-wave feminist one.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Declaration and Mill both demand removal of laws that confine women to a separate sphere and exclude them from public life, so law reflecting distinct public roles is rejected.

ban-interest.rationale: Usury law was not among first-wave aims and the opened sources do not mention it.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Racist arguments appeared among leaders, but the founding principles are universal rights and the abolitionist origins reject legal segregation; weak no.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The liberal mainstream treated the state as reformable through the vote, not as a class tool.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy is anachronistic for the period and unaddressed.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Stanton's disdain for immigrant voters suggests some nativism, but there is no movement-wide position.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy of elites to replace the population has no place in the movement's rights-based thought.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral system design is not documented as a first-wave concern.

national-mission.rationale: The sources give no sign that first-wave feminists held a mission to spread their country's government, though the movement itself was international.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Declaration lists a history of repeated injuries by men to establish absolute tyranny over women, and Mill calls it a subjection by custom and law, but it is framed as legal rather than structural patriarchy.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The movement protested exclusion from politics but made no general charge of corruption.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Wollstonecraft and Mill defend free individual choice and rational motherhood against state coercion; eugenic control is rejected, though later feminists were sometimes drawn to eugenics.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for state killings was not taken up in the sources.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement asked the state for legal reforms, education and equal protection, which goes beyond a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Racism existed among some leaders, but no movement doctrine discouraged intermarriage.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration states that all men and women are created equal and demands equal rights and privileges, which is this statement applied to women.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A debate within Marxism that the liberal-rights movement did not engage.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The characterisation of settler states is a later debate and absent from first-wave sources.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Mill demands a single legal order of equality, ending sex-based marriage and property law, so uniform rules are favoured, but religious-law exceptions were not discussed.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The Declaration places a woman's sphere under her conscience and her God, implying freedom of religion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Cattle slaughter law is a South Asian religious issue outside the movement's agenda.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Not addressed; Christian reformers were common.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Not applicable; the liberal mainstream rejects an expanding state.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration is modelled on the Declaration of Independence and complains of denying women any voice in the laws they must obey, which is the consent principle directly.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade balance goals are absent from the sources.

population-transfer.rationale: The movement's universal-rights basis rejects forced removal of any group.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The movement was largely non-violent but not absolutist; later militants and the state's use of law complicate it.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social Darwinist claims about struggle as progress are not part of the sources, and Mill's liberalism points elsewhere, so no clear line.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Banning parties is a twentieth-century constitutional device that the movement never addressed.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Mill's complaint that wives are bond-servants under arbitrary power, even when benign, is the non-domination idea, though he does not use the term.

separated-powers.rationale: The movement sought entry into representative institutions and relied on courts and legislatures; no source states a view on checks.

vanguard-party.rationale: Mass petitioning and the vote were the movement's methods, not a vanguard party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Poor women were a concern of some strands, but the middle-class mainstream did not organise around a priority to the poor.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing did not exist as a policy question for the movement.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law was a labour issue, and the opened sources tie first-wave feminism to no stance on it.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian explanations of poverty were not taken up in the sources, though birth-control campaigners sometimes touched the subject.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The universal-rights basis disfavors it, though racist remarks by some leaders existed.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The programme was to get women into elected office; lotteries were not proposed.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: A rights-first movement that claimed inalienable rights would resist suspending legal protections.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Food price controls were not part of the movement's demands.

party-controls-media.rationale: Mill's liberal case rests on open discussion, and the suffrage press was independent of government.

party-commands-army.rationale: Wollstonecraft's hostility to standing armies and the movement's constitutionalism reject party command of forces.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation periods were not a feminist question in the sources, though suffrage rules for naturalised men were mentioned only in passing.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Legislator pay was not discussed in the opened sources.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not addressed; suffrage groups sometimes backed party-neutral lobbying.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Supranational unions are modern and outside the movement's era.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The movement favoured legislatures and rights over executive power; weak no.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The Declaration protests exclusion from the ministry but does not address church government.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Declaration protests church-based subordination of women and demands equality before civil law, so clerical rule is opposed.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Term limits are not discussed in the sources.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials was a Progressive-era tool, but the sources do not tie the suffrage movement to a position.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy was not part of the women's-rights agenda.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Not addressed; liberal property views suggest no.

people-in-arms.rationale: Wollstonecraft opposes standing armies but there is no sign she or the movement favoured an armed citizenry.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification claims are unrelated to the movement's demands.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Rural versus urban morality is not discussed in the sources opened.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The movement demanded education for women and Wollstonecraft's main argument is that education enables reason and virtue.

death-penalty.rationale: Not a movement question; adherents had no common line.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic in form; first-wave views on sex education varied from purity campaigners to birth-control advocates.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The movement stressed reasoned education, but many adherents were devout, so only a weak no.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Social-purity and temperance feminists campaigned against obscenity; this is inferred rather than documented in the sources opened.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules by descent were not discussed apart from women's rights over nationality, which the sources do not cover.

minority-language-support.rationale: Language rights were not discussed in the sources, except national language frictions such as Swiss regional divisions.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The Declaration protects conscience but does not address exemption from general laws.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill's liberalism praises diversity of ways of living, but this statement is from On Liberty rather than from the opened Subjection text, so confidence is low.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt was outside the movement's concerns.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Post-colonial economic transformation was no part of first-wave aims.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Constitution-writing procedure was not discussed, though some national movements wanted women in new assemblies.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement's central aim was gaining political freedom and it would not accept suspending it.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Global aid duties were not raised by first-wave feminists in the opened sources.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not discuss how heads of state are chosen.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central bank design is not addressed in the sources.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial concessions are not a theme in first-wave feminism.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Declaration treats property as a right a woman should hold; subordination to the common good is not stated, though the German strand spoke of a common good.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The Soviet Union postdates most of the movement, and no stance is documented.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental risk policy is anachronistic for the movement.

collective-defense.rationale: Mutual defence treaties are twentieth-century and not discussed in the sources.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Declaration protests church subordination of women, but curbing church property was not proposed.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Whether a head of state stands above party politics is not discussed in the sources.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Use of force against secession is not discussed in the sources.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special regional autonomy arrangements were not an issue for the movement.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Wollstonecraft criticises monarchy and hereditary honours, and the Declaration appeals to natural right rather than divine rule.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax rate structure is not addressed in the sources.

character-from-environment.rationale: Strands split: Mill calls woman's nature an artificial product of upbringing and Wollstonecraft blames education for women's faults, while the maternalist wing argued for a distinct innate female nature.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mill argues that despotism cannot be defended in the family or the state and demands equal legal subjection for all.

space-expansion.rationale: Space expansion is anachronistic for the movement.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed constitution theory is not part of first-wave writing, which focused on extending the franchise.

leader-cult.rationale: Wollstonecraft's attack on rank and hereditary honour and the movement's egalitarianism reject leader worship.

equal-parenting.rationale: The Declaration protests custody law that favours fathers, but equal-time presumptions are modern and the movement also valued motherhood.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: This is an internal Marxist-Leninist debate that first-wave feminism did not engage.

land-redistribution.rationale: The movement sought women's right to hold land, not seizure of estates.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return rights are not discussed in the sources.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Declaration places religion in the individual's conscience; punishment for leaving a faith contradicts it.

women-must-cover.rationale: The movement demanded that women be free and equal in public life and conscience, and no source suggests compelling women's dress.

common-currency.rationale: Currency unions are modern and not discussed.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-ethnic political unions were not part of the movement's agenda.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority self-government in schools and culture is not discussed in the sources opened.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The movement demanded rights in the countries women lived in rather than separate states, but it is not a statement about minorities.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The mainstream grounded change in Enlightenment ideas of equality, not in production; socialist wings differed.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy was not discussed by first-wave feminists in the opened sources.

no-bailouts.rationale: Public rescue of firms is not discussed in the sources.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The movement claimed inalienable rights, the kind that majority votes of men could not remove, so courts constraining majorities is favoured.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: First-wave aim was formal equality, such as the vote, not mandated parity, which belongs to later waves.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic colonial blocs were no part of the movement's demands.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade agreement standards are modern and not addressed.

moral-incentives.rationale: Moral incentives replacing material ones were a socialist-state idea absent from the sources.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The movement worked through mass petitioning and persuasion, not a small armed group.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred from Wollstonecraft's attack on hereditary honours; the suffrage movements did not campaign against titles and some leaders were aristocrats.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Curriculum emphasis on one's own nation was not raised in the opened first-wave sources.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Some suffragists accepted colonial hierarchies, but sources show no movement doctrine; split.

patriotic-education.rationale: Wollstonecraft wanted education to teach civic virtue, but pride in flags and anthems is not discussed.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation by public bodies was not an issue for the movement.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The Marxist crisis debate is not a first-wave feminist theme.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Post-imperial influence policy is outside the movement's agenda.

delink-world-market.rationale: Dependency theory postdates the movement and is not discussed.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The Leninist labour-aristocracy thesis was not taken up by the liberal mainstream.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Declaration's complaint is exclusion from colleges, professions and offices on grounds of sex, so a freedom to refuse service or hire on any grounds contradicts its principle, though not directly addressing private discrimination.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Declaration frames women's claims as inalienable rights that governments must respect and extend, so entrenched rights fit, though no first-wave text proposes entrenchment mechanisms.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Colonial treaty law is not discussed in the sources.

elective-rulers.rationale: Inferred from the demand for the vote; American suffragists were republicans, but British suffragists did not oppose the monarchy.

minority-veto.rationale: The movement sought majority voting rules open to women, not individual vetoes.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The Declaration echoes the Declaration of Independence's right to resist tyranny, but resistance meant civil disobedience, not removal.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The movement targeted legislatures for the vote, implying legislative sovereignty, with parliament as the place to win rights.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Many reformers of the era backed anti-cruelty causes, but opened sources do not document it.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Same inference: humane treatment while allowing use.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wollstonecraft criticises the idle rich as vain and helpless; philanthropy by privileged women was common, but no single position.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement's whole project was women's entry into public and political life, as the franchise demand shows.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Not addressed; later critical theory idea.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: World-systems theory is modern and absent from first-wave writings.

native-born-offices.rationale: Nativism existed among some leaders but no movement position.

party-own-road.rationale: This concerns communist parties and is not applicable to the suffrage movement.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Development strategy is not addressed in the first-wave sources.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentist claims are not part of the sources on women's rights.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Indigenous leadership is not discussed in the opened sources.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Fascism emerged as the movement was ending, and the sources contain no stance.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The comparison of fascism and communism postdates first-wave feminism.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Suffrage leaders came from abolitionism and treated slavery as central, but the movement took no formal position on this historiography.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument controversy is anachronistic and not addressed.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; the movement's focus was women's legal disabilities.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: The movement focused on husbands' legal power over wives, so equal-seriousness symmetry would be disputed; no direct source.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: First-wave demands rest on universal rights, not civilizational particularism.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Wollstonecraft calls standing armies incompatible with freedom, so a political guardian role for the military is rejected.

paid-care-work.rationale: A later demand; first-wave feminists valued motherhood but sought legal reform, not wages for domestic work.

filial-duty.rationale: Wollstonecraft argues for reciprocal duties in family relations, but this is not a movement stance.

office-by-exam.rationale: Wollstonecraft and Mill want careers open by ability, which exams serve, but no source discusses exams.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Mill notes that refusing divorce makes a wife a slave and the Declaration protests divorce laws regardless of women's happiness, though first-wave feminists differed on easy divorce.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Imperative mandates are a council-democracy idea outside the movement's programme.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is anachronistic and not discussed.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The movement demanded women's right to own property and rejected community-owned land held only by use.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Taxation without representation grievance implies parliamentary control of the budget, but not stated.

single-official-language.rationale: Language policy is not addressed in the sources beyond Swiss regional divisions.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Foreign land ownership is not discussed in the sources.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Wollstonecraft decries vanity and luxury, but there is no movement position.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: First-wave feminism aimed at formal equality of law, not the substantive equality later waves sought, so outcome-based tests of discrimination are not its stance.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Covert support for insurgents is outside the movement's concerns.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Bloc discipline intervention concerns Cold War politics, long after first-wave feminism.

corporate-influence.rationale: Lobbying and campaign finance by firms are not discussed in the opened sources.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Foreign funding of NGOs is a recent debate, though early international suffrage alliances relied on cross-border support; no stance is documented.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: State incentives for births are not discussed, and birth control campaigners such as Jacobs favoured women's own control.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local property purchase limits are modern and unaddressed.

job-guarantee.rationale: State employer of last resort is not discussed in first-wave sources.

democratic-peace.rationale: Wollstonecraft's link of free institutions to peace and the hostility to armies suggest it, but she does not state this.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Declaration insists women must obey laws they had no voice in making, implying obedience requires consent, but it did not deny a general duty; split.

non-intervention.rationale: Absolute non-intervention is not discussed in the sources.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure was a labour question, not a feminist one in the sources.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: A conspiracy theory about a minority has no place in a universal-rights movement.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Mill reforms marriage law into equal partnership rather than abolishing it, and most first-wave women sought legal marriage with rights.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Freedom of information law postdates the movement.

local-production.rationale: Localist economics is not discussed in the sources.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movement created formal associations and societies such as national suffrage associations and the International Alliance of Women.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The ranking of domestic and international law is modern and not addressed.

religious-nation.rationale: A rights-based movement defines the community by citizenship, not religion, though Christian reformers were many.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Tribute systems are unrelated to the movement.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Regional fiscal arrangements are not discussed in the sources.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The demand that women keep their wages and property supports private personal belongings, but community of production was not addressed.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism as an opponent postdates most of the movement, and no stance appears.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Public service delivery models are not discussed in the sources.

religion-illusion.rationale: Wollstonecraft defends God's goodness and the movement had many pious women, so describing religion as an illusion is rejected.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Not addressed; split between liberal and socialist wings.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The mainstream sought legal and political equality, while socialist-aligned women disagreed; the mainstream view is that law reform suffices.

socialized-care.rationale: The mainstream did not propose socialising domestic work; motherhood in the home was valued.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism is not discussed in the sources.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaties with internal nations are not discussed in the sources.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Third-way economics is not part of first-wave feminism, which was silent on system choice.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Historic claims to land are not discussed in the sources.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Anachronistic, but a universal-rights movement rejects it; weakly cited.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Not addressed; 19th-century morals would favour it but the movement did not campaign on it, so split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Mill defends free discussion and the movement was itself an opposition demanding a voice, so suppression is rejected.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Declaration places religion in conscience and protests church authority over women, so punishing blasphemy is rejected.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Colonial economic governance is not addressed, though critics note first-wave feminists often accepted colonial hierarchies.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: This is an Islamic legal doctrine outside the movement's scope.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Religious law as test of rulers is opposed by the Declaration's rights framework.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The movement demanded an equal voice in deciding laws, but its method was representative franchise, so only weak agreement.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The first-wave focus on gender and the vote is criticised by later scholars for ignoring race and class, so it did not hold the intersectional view.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Gender identity law is anachronistic, and the first-wave sources treat only women and men.

assisted-dying.rationale: Assisted dying is not discussed in first-wave sources.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The movement's sources do not address the left-right spectrum.

alienated-labor.rationale: Marxist idea; the mainstream sought the right to paid work, not to condemn it.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The universal-rights framework rejects it, though colonial attitudes existed.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Declaration derives authority from natural rights and the consent of the governed, and rejects apostolic authority claims.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Dress rules in state institutions are not discussed in the sources.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Nondisclosure agreements are a modern workplace issue unrelated to first-wave aims.

social-market-economy.rationale: Economic order was left open by the movement, so no stance is derivable.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Wollstonecraft opposes standing armies but does not call for abolition of all forces.

rich-first.rationale: The movement's equal-rights principle rejects stages in which some groups are held back.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Suffrage movements split over wartime stance, with some pacifist and others, such as British suffragettes in 1914, backing their governments, so no common line.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Social-purity wings campaigned against obscene material, while liberals such as Mill favoured free expression, so adherents divide.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Critics note first-wave feminism often accepted Western and colonial hierarchies, while universalist principles pull the other way.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Annexation law is outside the movement's concerns.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign investment screening is not discussed in the sources.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Hereditary rule contradicts the natural-rights equality the Declaration of Sentiments claims; Wollstonecraft and Mill attack inherited privilege, though succession was not a campaign issue.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Never addressed; inferred only from the movement's silence on economics beyond married women's right to property and earnings.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement left economics and foreign finance open, so no side can be inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: Suffragists demanded the vote for women on grounds of equal citizenship, though some Anglo-American campaigners accepted property qualifications as a stepping stone, so the rejection is not absolute.

domination-women-nature.rationale: An ecofeminist idea of a later era; first-wave writers sought legal equality and did not link women's status to nature, so none is inferred.

reification.rationale: Marxist theory the liberal first wave did not use; inferred from its Enlightenment liberal basis, which treats market relations as free contract.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Not addressed; suffragists used petitions and their own periodicals, and liberal and labour-linked adherents differed on class power.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Mill and Wollstonecraft argue from Enlightenment ideals of law over arbitrary power, and the Declaration indicts arbitrary tyranny, though the point is not made as a general doctrine.

racial-franchise.rationale: Its natural-rights basis supports universal suffrage, but white suffrage leaders in the United States sometimes accepted or promoted racial restriction, so adherents were not uniform.

online-participation.rationale: Anachronistic; nothing in the sources bears on it, and none can be inferred from the movement's demand for participation.

open-government-data.rationale: Anachronistic and never addressed by the movement.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Inferred from the demand for fairer marriage law and individual rights in marriage; the sources do not address religious restrictions.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Inferred from liberal equal-rights principles; the movement did not address consumer boycotts of minorities.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement sought representation through the franchise and did not discuss sortition.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Stanton's Woman's Bible and Declaration criticised scriptural arguments for women's subordination, and Mill and Wollstonecraft dismissed custom and authority, though many adherents stayed orthodox.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred: Wollstonecraft attacks the power of hereditary wealth, but the movement was liberal and gave no settled view on wealth inequality.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Anachronistic: the movement never addressed open service by gay people, and its Victorian-era norms would have opposed it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: the movement was mostly religious and sought equality before the law, not state promotion of any belief or unbelief.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred from its liberal reliance on law and courts to secure rights; it never proposed abolishing police or prisons.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred: it demanded equal individual voting rights for all citizens under majority rule, not guaranteed shares for communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Women's philanthropy was central to many activists, while others pressed for public provision; the movement did not settle the question.

term-limits.rationale: Inferred: the liberal thinkers it drew on wanted voters free to choose; Mill valued experienced representatives.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred: the campaign was for each woman to cast her own ballot, so delegating votes runs against its aims.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Anachronistic: the movement never addressed extinction risk, so this is inferred from its focus on present rights and reform.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments protests that women are kept in a subordinate place in the Church and excluded from the ministry.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Declaration says a married woman is made civilly dead and promises obedience to her husband as her master, and Mill attacks the husband's legal power as a form of slavery.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's franchise demand was for women as citizens, and nothing in its sources speaks to non-citizen residents.

rent-control.rationale: Inferred from the movement's liberal property and contract outlook; rent caps were never a first-wave issue.

abolish-ip.rationale: Never addressed; inferred from the movement's liberal property-rights framing, though women authors depended on copyright.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Never addressed; inferred from the movement's liberal preference for voluntary association and persuasion over state drilling.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement predates nuclear weapons and has no recorded stance.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Not addressed; Wollstonecraft attacked standing armies but foreign bases were not an issue for the movement.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Anachronistic; the term and the practice of state recognition postdate the movement.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Inferred from Wollstonecraft's attack on hereditary rank and idleness and the demand that women earn and keep their own earnings.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Pacifism was a minority strand; most suffragists accepted lawful force, so adherents mostly reject an absolute ban.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Its natural-rights basis was universal, not tied to national origins; inferred from the Declaration's appeal to all men and women.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Mill argued women's character was shaped by custom, but the movement accepted sex difference as given and contested only its legal consequences.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: The movement organised around women as a single class with shared grievances, as the Declaration's list of wrongs shows, even if later critics noted its race and class blind spots.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Suffrage campaigners honoured their own movement's sacrifices, but veneration of national dead as martyrs was no part of its liberal outlook.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Its case rested on rights, reason and interests, though a religious and temperance wing framed reform morally; inferred from the Declaration's natural-rights language.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Not addressed; neither a nationalist idea nor one the movement took up.

culture-before-state.rationale: Not addressed; the movement sought political rights within existing states.

god-not-male.rationale: Adherents split: some, like Stanton, challenged religious authority, while many devout members kept traditional language; the Declaration criticises only women's exclusion from the church.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: The Declaration protests the church's exclusion of women and the use of scripture against them; inferred that adherents would set aside diminishing teachings, though many were devout.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Its demand was equal access to trades and the professions for all, not group-based economic roles; inferred from the Declaration.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no recorded stance on regional borders.

independent-unions.rationale: Trade unions were not a first-wave concern; the movement's demands were legal and political.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: A liberal rights movement that did not debate the definition of socialism; adherents ranged from labour-linked to middle-class reformers.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Never addressed; the movement's demands were legal and political, and no stance on public services is recorded.

second-chamber.rationale: Constitutional design of legislatures was not its issue; it sought the vote under existing institutions.

municipal-property.rationale: Inferred: the Declaration and Mill demand individual property rights for women, which sits against community-owned productive property.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Never addressed; no stance on confederal structures is recorded.

family-wage.rationale: Not a first-wave demand; the movement sought women's own earnings and access to professions, and adherents were not united on family wages.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Anachronistic; medical regulation was not an issue for the movement.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred from the sources.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred from the sources.

online-anonymity.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred from the sources.

person-over-state.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments and Mill ground women's claims in natural rights and individual liberty, which no state or custom may override.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Inferred: Wollstonecraft appeals to reason and the soul and many suffragists were religious, though others such as Stanton criticised the churches.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Never addressed; campaigns ran at both state and national level without a stance on entrenching regional powers.

gm-crops.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

dense-cities.rationale: Anachronistic; no stance can be inferred.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Inferred: the movement rested on universal natural rights, though its racist arguments and the Fifteenth Amendment split show some adherents did put white interests first.

racial-pride.rationale: Not addressed in the movement's founding texts; adherents were divided, with abolitionist roots on one side and racist suffrage arguments on the other.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Never a core issue; Wollstonecraft attacks standing armies, but the movement had no settled doctrine on the use of force.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from its civic, rights-based liberal outlook rather than ethnic nationhood.

communal-electorates.rationale: Inferred from its demand for equal citizenship and a common franchise for women, not separate communal voting.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from its focus on legal reform at home rather than nationalist anxieties.

free-public-college.rationale: Not addressed directly; it demanded women's access to education, which suggests support for open public universities.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Not addressed; the movement predates environmental politics and has no basis for a clear answer.

future-generations.rationale: Not addressed; the movement predates environmental politics and has no basis for a clear answer.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Adherents were split between equal-rights arguments (Wollstonecraft, Mill) and maternalist claims that women's moral influence should count.

arms-reduction.rationale: Not addressed directly; inferred from the many suffragists who were also peace campaigners.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from its Enlightenment liberal emphasis on open, accountable government.

capital-controls.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from its liberal individualist leaning, with no stated view on capital movement.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The movement did not take up who may bear arms; Wollstonecraft attacked standing armies but the sources show no stance on armed groups.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Many suffragists were pacifist but others backed the First World War effort, so a call for soldiers to refuse orders is inferred as not mainstream.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Women's labor organizing existed, but the movement's core demands were legal and political and the sources record no stance on bargaining.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; the demands were legal and political and tax credits did not exist.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Fiscal rules were never addressed by the movement, and nothing in its principles settles the question.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The movement left economics and international affairs open, and some branches were tied to empire while others criticized it.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments and suffrage campaigns sought entry to the existing franchise and legal order, not its destruction.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Economic systems were left open by the movement; its demand was legal equality within the existing economy.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Natural-resource accounting is anachronistic and the movement did not address it.

sacred-nation.rationale: The movement was rooted in universal natural rights rather than the nation, although some suffragists used nationalist arguments; inferred.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student loans did not exist and the movement's education demand was for access, so this is left neutral.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; its focus was on women's legal status.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments rests on natural rights shared by all and Wollstonecraft held reason is common to both sexes, though Mill saw women's nature as shaped by custom.

public-service-media.rationale: Broadcasting did not exist in the movement's period, and its principles do not settle the question.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; the movement included freethinkers and devout churchwomen and took no position on religious truth.

farm-price-support.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; the movement's demands were legal and political and the sources record no stance on farm policy.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources record no first-wave position on nuclear arms.

workers-own-party.rationale: Suffrage leaders worked through nonpartisan and cross-class campaigns; the sources show no consensus on a separate workers' party.

ban-fgm.rationale: Inferred from the movement's attack on women's subjection and its call for protection of women's persons in law, since FGM was not a campaign issue.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments objects that a married woman is civilly dead and loses her property, and Mill demands equal legal capacity to own property.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Never addressed by the movement; no position can be inferred from its legal-equality principles.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources record no stance on pollution, and liberal natural-rights thought could support either liability or regulation.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Inferred from Enlightenment natural-rights thought and the attack on custom and hereditary rank, which count against customary chiefs.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources record no first-wave stance on environmental policy versus liberty.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Not addressed; the movement's demands were about legal equality and not about criminal sentencing.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no stance on immigrants' language can be inferred from its sources.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Right-to-work laws and union membership were not first-wave issues; inferred as no stance.

voter-id.rationale: Voter identification was not debated; the movement's concern was extending the franchise, so no direction is inferred.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Inferred from the movement's liberal equal-rights principles; Stanton-era critics of church authority and church-going reformers differed, so only weakly.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Inferred from Mill's and the suffragists' view that legitimacy rests on representation and consent, though they also valued the policies representation would produce.

premarital-sex.rationale: Wollstonecraft and most mainstream suffragists upheld chastity and marital fidelity; a few radicals dissented.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Inferred from liberal civil-liberties commitments and reliance on petition, press and public meetings to win rights.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Not a first-wave issue; adherents ranged from laissez-faire liberals to labour-linked reformers.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments names denial of the franchise as the first grievance, and the vote was the movement's defining demand.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Stanton and some radicals blamed church teaching, while many suffragists were devout and drew on religious arguments; adherents were split.

race-social-construct.rationale: Anachronistic: the scientific concept of race as social construct postdates the movement, and many suffragists held racial views of their time while others were abolitionists.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Dedicated equality agencies were not a first-wave demand; the movement sought legal equality, so no stance is inferred.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the Enlightenment natural-rights thinking the movement used, which supported property rights, though it did not discuss first claim.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Wollstonecraft's attack on standing armies and the movement's peace-linked reform outlook.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Seneca Falls attacked church limits on women, and some leaders later criticised literal biblical readings, but adherents were divided; inferred.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the demand for women's equal political voice and equal participation.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Not addressed; the movement was liberal and did not support planned economies; inferred.

indirect-election.rationale: The movement demanded the franchise for women on equal terms with men, which fits direct election; inferred.

national-church-status.rationale: Seneca Falls protested church limits on women, and liberal equality implies no special state church; inferred.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed; the sources give no stance on minority territorial autonomy.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the consent-of-the-governed framing of the Declaration of Sentiments.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Not addressed; the sources give no stance on colonial borders.

simple-living.rationale: Not addressed; the movement left lifestyle and economics open.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from liberal equal-rights thinking and no sign of such restrictions.

equal-conscription.rationale: Suffragists were split over whether duties like military service followed from equal rights; inferred.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The movement never addressed national homelands as such; anachronistic.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The movement rested on natural rights and due process, so killing suspects without trial would be rejected; inferred.

close-ties-china.rationale: The question is anachronistic and the movement left foreign policy open.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The movement left nationality and foreign policy open, so no stance follows; anachronistic.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The movement left economics open and its liberals differed on common ownership; inferred.

self-ownership.rationale: Wollstonecraft and Mill argued women have rights over their own persons and earnings, and the Declaration condemned wives' loss of both.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Tax policy was left open by the movement; anachronistic.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The movement left welfare design open; anachronistic.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The movement worked through associations, petitions and legislatures, so bypassing groups runs against its method; inferred.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Liberal equal-rights thought opposes legal privilege for favoured groups; inferred.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Many leaders pressed for law free of church control, though suffragists were religious and split; inferred.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Enlightenment liberal thought looked to progress and reason, not a return to ancestral values; inferred.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments objected to divorce law that favoured husbands, and Mill backed fairer marriage law; a no-consent rule is an inference.

national-resource-control.rationale: The movement left resource ownership open; anachronistic.

missingStatements.text: Women should have the same right to vote and hold public office as men.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments names denial of the elective franchise as its first grievance, and the suffrage was the movement's defining aim.

missingStatements.text: Married women should have the same legal right as men to own property, keep their earnings and make contracts.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration protests that a married woman is civilly dead and loses all right in property even to her wages, and Mill attacks coverture as bond-servitude.

missingStatements.text: Women should have the same access as men to higher education and to the professions.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration complains that all colleges are closed to women and the professions barred, and Mill and Wollstonecraft both demand equal education.

notes: First-wave feminism was a legal-equality movement; adherents split on abortion, temperance and moral reform, race and class, so answers outside gender and law are mostly low-confidence inferences. Leaders such as Stanton and Stone voiced racist and nativist arguments in the Fifteenth Amendment dispute.
